newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - China's GITIC goes to U.S..
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - China's GITIC goes to U.S..

text.p: Asian debt markets were quiet on Friday after some action in the U.S. overnight with a bond issue for a Chinese entity.
China's Guangdong International Trust and Investment (GITIC) placed a US$200 million bond into the 144a market via lead manager Merrill Lynch.
The 8.75 percent 20-year bond was priced at 99.72 to yield 8.78 percent or 195 basis points over the old U.S. Treasury 30-year bond.
GITIC is rated Baa2 by Moody's Investors Service and BBB-minus by Standard and Poor's Corp.

GITIC usually does its borrowing via loans, but bankers said it has other capital markets issues to its credit including a US$150 million floating rate note launched in 1993 and a US$150 million bond privately placed in the U.S. in 1994.
Next up for China in the U.S. market is a Yankee bond for State Development Bank of China, which is expected to be about US$300 million in size.

State Development Bank launched its debut capital markets issue in February of this year, a 4.0 percent 30 billion yen bond due in 2006. Bankers complained at the time that the bond was unrealistically priced.
Elsewhere, bankers in Asia are awaiting the deluge of South Korean bank paper that is expected to hit the market before year end. Some US$700 million could be offered, they said.
Syndicate managers said the timing is bad because many banks have filled up their books with about as much South Korean paper as they planned to take this year.
"Banks are fairly full up at the moment and we're seeing things start to slow down," said a syndicate manager at a European bank in Hong Kong.
"But the outlook is fairly positive for Korea and after year-end there will be more buying," he said.

Banks have been willing to hold onto South Korean bank paper on the view that spreads will continue to narrow, even though many traders believe a fair amount of tightening related to Korea's invitation to join the Organization for Economic Cooperation already has happened.
That's because Korean credits still are priced generously compared with similarly rated names from other countries.
In news from Hong Kong, Societe Generale Asia has privately placed an HK$250 million six-month floating rate certificate of deposit issue for Wing Lung Bank.
There was speculation earlier this week that Wing Lung was looking for HK$500 million.
The Hong Kong Monetary Authority today announced that it would tender its debut 10-year Exchange Fund Note issue on October 28.
The monetary authority announced some time ago that it hoped to extend the government debt yield curve out to 10 years before the end of 1996. At present, the longest-maturity EFN is seven years.
